title: The Joy of Collaboration Over Control

turns.speaker: Thomas Jepson-Lay
paras: Excellent. Welcome. Hello, everybody. Kim, Ali. Good to see you again. And Susan, we're joined by your presence. Thank you so much. It's a real pleasure. Thank you for having me. The Secretary General for the Order of St John International. Is that correct? That's it. Yeah. Excellent. Brilliant. Perfect. Maybe a quick introduction from your side on exactly where the Order of St John works, what it is for those who might not be familiar with it.

turns.speaker: Susan le Jeune d'Allegeershecque
paras: Yes, so it's an unusual organisation in that we started more than 900 years ago in Holy Land where St John Hospitals, as they were called in those days, provided medical care to pilgrims and others who were in the Holy Land. And from that it became an order of chivalry, was disbanded under the Reformation in this country, and then was restarted during Victorian era provided the first ever ambulances to victims of industrial accidents effectively in the industrial revolution so mines, railways, mills and factories and today we're present in 44 countries around the world most of them in countries of the British Commonwealth and the United States and so that means Asia Pacific, Australia, Africa, the Caribbean and North America.

And the aims of the charity, which is both a charity and an order of chivalry these days, is to provide healthcare, community healthcare, so medical responses to needs in the community, but also fundamentally and right at the heart of what we do is first aid. So we are the people who provide pre-hospital care and training to others to allow them to provide pre-hospital care. So that includes things like CPR, use of defibrillators first aid at events. So you will have seen us in this country at large sporting and other events providing help. And those people save lives on a daily basis wherever we work. And we also train people in companies and schools and teachers and various others who might need to use first aid in the course of their daily life.
And then the community healthcare is very much adapted to the countries where we're working.

turns.speaker: Thomas Jepson-Lay
paras: Brilliant, thank you. Yeah, you said it. I'm very familiar with St John's ambulance. It's part of community events. It's almost a feature of the event and I've been the recipient of many of your trainings over the years and have been able to utilise them. So having been in those encounters, it's been encouraging and confidence-inspiring to have had the training from your team. So I'm I'm very familiar and comfortable. But my familiarity with St John is at a local community level here in the UK. And you're talking about the international arm of the organisation. You listed a whole bunch of countries that you're working in there. So within the multi-lateral aid space, there's the term localisation, which is shifting the power to locally led entities.
It's a topic that's been around for well over a decade now. What does locally led action or localisation mean for St John as it operates around the world?

turns.speaker: Susan le Jeune d'Allegeershecque
paras: So we haven't had to localise because we've always been a locally led organisation. So I think you're right. Many people know us as their local St John ambulance. Very few people are aware of the fact that we are a global organisation. So whereas other international organisations like ours are pretty well known, we're unfortunately quite a well-kept secret internationally, but we are a federation so we're made up of 44 simply 45 independent charities with oversight from a board in London, but those each act independently and they are locally led and locally focused. So there is no question of anybody sitting here or elsewhere in our network coming in and telling the people in Malawi or Solomon Islands what it is they need and how they need to do it.

And I think that is one of our huge advantages. So both our staff and fundamentally the most important part of our delivery are volunteers of whom there are nearly 200,000 around the world, other people who deliver and they are drawn from the local community and they deliver to their friends, colleagues, families in the local community. So, that is, you can imagine that also has its own challenges because in a loose federation your control and your oversight has to be exercised mainly by cooperation, not coercion. And in an organisation which has a lot of volunteers, some of them young people, there are obviously issues around safeguarding, there can be issues around safeguarding.

And also if you're providing medical care, you want to make absolutely sure that quality of what you're delivering is really good because it's people's lives that are at risk. I mean I'm not suggesting for a minute that any one of our organisations doesn't do it correctly but I think that tension between the benefits of it being this loose federation of independent charities and the need to have that oversight is one of the things that my team and I grapple with on the daily basis.

turns.speaker: Kim Kucinskas
paras: Susan, do you think it's interesting because, you know, we've been talking about versions of localisation, locally led development in with different language for, I would say longer than 10 years, right, Thomas? I mean, it was for a long, long time. And it's always interesting to talk to people who work in organisations where it was designed that way. Cause it's like, well, it's so obvious. This is how you do it. There are so many organisations right now that are trying to maintain their legitimacy and their mission and their value while kind of transforming. So are you following, have you been following that conversation I guess is a question?

turns.speaker: Susan le Jeune d'Allegeershecque
paras: I know a little about that conversation from my previous life where I worked in the diplomatic service for over 30 years. So it's a conversation with which I'm familiar.

turns.speaker: Kim Kucinskas
paras: And then what are the lessons coming from an organisation that has kind of always been in this space for others that are looking to kind of transform or that are trying to even just do baby steps.

turns.speaker: Susan le Jeune d'Allegeershecque
paras: So I think one of the issues is that you need to be out, we'll come on to leadership later I think, but one of the issues that you need to be absolutely clear about is the quality of local leadership really makes a difference here. So you can't assume that you've got the right people doing it and you can't assume that those people who, you can't necessarily assume that people who've been the right person in the past or the right person today and getting that change embedded can be really hard because people feel very strongly about this charity. Many of them have been involved in it since they were five years old as cadets and have grown up through our youth programmes and are still there and they're in their later years.

So that I think is a huge challenge and I think that's something that you can't assume is going to work, so having the right people in place. I think also being very clear that what works in one place doesn't always work in another. Sometimes the principles are the right ones, but actually how you implement that on the ground can be very different. I think the other thing that we grapple with constantly is making sure that every part of the organisation has a voice in defining our strategies and our priorities and that when things are difficult for them, they have ways of feeling it back and being listened to.

One of the recent developments with St John is the implementation of a region, it's not a structure but a regional approach. So we were very conscious of the fact that the distance between somebody sitting in the Solomon Islands or Barbados and us in London, if they wanted to, A, be helped to improve, or B, articulate concerns. It sometimes felt like a long time of the Americas, Europe, the Middle East and Africa, and then Asia-Pacific. And those are informal structures. They're not government structures. They're not extra levels of bureaucracy, but a senior leader in each of those three regions has taken on the job of bringing them together.

And they act as the sort of improvement and support mechanism and then some of the more hard-edged policing and enforcement when that's necessary comes from my office in London and I think that that's really important because that that that distance can be hugely challenging and I think the other thing it does is it's building up cooperation within the region so you've got you've got you know somebody in New Zealand, St John in Fiji, because they're closer, they culturally are more aware of the things that are needed. But it might also be that somebody in Barbados has some really good information or practice or whatever experience that might help the person in Barbados.
So also fostering those links between the various organisations which don't involve necessarily the centre, it's a really important part of how we've done it.

turns.speaker: Ali Al Mokdad
paras: Out of curiosity, I'm just thinking that you mentioned those local roots and the localised programming at country level and also those regional structure and of course the international office or had a quarter. turns.speaker: Susan le Jeune d'Allegeershecque
paras: So I think the important thing is to define very clearly who does what. So I think at the regional level it is very clear that they are not there to police, they're not there to wave a big stick, they're not there to enforce standards, they're there to encourage development and foster improvements and be the softer side of leadership if you like. In my office we also provide support, particularly financial support, when the rights or projects are presented to us, but our role is much more on the standards, governance, guidance side, and I think that's very clear. It means that we don't get to do the nice stuff quite as often, but you know that's fine.

It works exactly the sort of people who deliver that in the way it should be done. I think we've also made sure that we have information, best practice available globally. So we've recently developed a hub of a resource hub where all our best practices available and anybody can have access to that. So that's we see that as the role of my team in London as providing those tools to allow every establishment within the St John family to flourish. We are now fundraising probably for the first time ever seriously in my office in London and that is in order to provide resources for the individual establishments, many of which are not in any position to do that.

So we're not doing it and patronising here's a handout way, which is without wanting to sort of generalise and diss what has gone before. And it was a bit like that in the past. So somebody would come to us and ask for some money and we just, not quite, but it would be handed out to them, but without any sense of a sustainable plan for what that money or what those resources would be used for. So we're trying to make all that much more professional and much more valuable both in art for us, but all particularly for the establishments concerned. And we've just set up a brand new small grant fund for every establishment.

We've just given out the first grant, in fact. And that's a very, very quick process so that the establishments will put in a proposal to us and within two weeks they'll get a yes or no. They're relatively small scale projects, but they have to have the proper planning and everything to explain what they're doing and that that we feel and the people who decide are all, I mean, you will all be familiar with this, but they're all drawn from our community. They're not people in my office. So you have practitioners from around the globe who come together as a panel and take decisions on the proposals when they come to them.
This is really fascinating. You've just list, I'm not sure, Kim and Ali are thinking the same sort of thing.

turns.speaker: Susan le Jeune d'Allegeershecque
paras: Okay. Shall we do the joy first? Please. I can do the joy first. So, I mean, I brought to this job, I've been in the job for five years and I brought to the job a lot of experience of working precisely using persuasion and collaboration rather than coercion. I think that it is one of the joys of this organisation that we don't control, we don't try to control and we allow others to flourish. So I see it almost as you know letting your children leave home and go to university and then have their own lives. I mean, it feels a bit like that. It wasn't always like that.

It used to be that the central priory, because that's what we call them, because establishments in England control the world from here. And in the late 1990s, a deliberate decision was made to let that go. And so we established a very small international office, there's sort of 15 of us here. And then the the independence was underlined and reinforced. Where we had a bit of a problem in the governance space was with our smaller organisations. So we have 12 really big ones, and they are apart from the eye hospital in Jerusalem and the priories of South Africa and Kenya. They're all in what you would describe as global North countries.

Then we have all the other smaller ones, most of whom are in the global South. We didn't have an institutional governance framework governing our relationship with those smaller establishments and that was problematical for us because they couldn't see the benefit of what we did for them and we felt that we didn't really have any levers to pull or any way to channel our support to them properly. So over the last 18 months or so we have written and now implemented a relationship agreement with every single one of those smaller organisations and you know you might have thought that there would be a lot of resistance to that because they could see if you if you're looking at it from a negative perspective that they were giving up control that we would be crawling all over them and requiring them to do things and and and there is that sort of post-colonial you know concern that it might look as if we were trying to do that.

In fact extraordinarily and this was a huge surprise to me and my colleagues, every single one of them apart from three welcomed this with open arms and they welcomed it because they wanted to have that relationship defined, they wanted to know what they could expect from us and they wanted to know what was expected from them in return and also to know that the support, they were support for them from us or at the regional level to allow them to to get to the point that in an ideal world, every single one of our establishments would be gold standard and everything they do. So that's been, I mean, I think that's a really, I mean, surprisingly easy for us to implement and it's been very positive.

And I think that's a model which is, it's not a particularly long document, but it's one which covers all the bases. And it also has a small bit of it, which says, if you don't sign up to this, or if you don't abide by our values, or if you don't read the standards, or if you're not transparent about your finances or whatever else it is, then there are things that will happen. And again, this is, I'm telling you to suck eggs now, but this is really important for an organisation like ours, where reputation and trust is so important to the way we operate. You know, if you're going to be calling it somebody in to train you in first aid, you want to know that you're getting people who are really good at what they do.

And so our smaller establishments now, I think, have a much better sense that they, you know, they have a dog in this fight, that actually maintaining the reputation means as much to them and that they are responsible for that in the same way as the prior in New Zealand and Australia or Canada. So that's been a, and for me, actually, you know, it's like any leadership thing. If your ego is not massive, then actually one of the most satisfying things you can do is to see the people that work with you flourish and sometimes overtake you. And I think that's one of the things about this new phase in our existence that it's seeing others flourish.
Basically it's about serving more lives. And that's why not having the control is actually quite liberating and I think it's a model which works really well for us.

turns.speaker: Susan le Jeune d'Allegeershecque
paras: It also means that I think that the board, we have a small board here in London which is made up of a rotating group of people from the various large establishments who come through and change over on a regular basis, they also have to be prepared to take tough decisions when things are not going right so you know and that that has been lacking in the past as well so the every part of this family needs to see that playing by the rules has benefits not playing by the rules has disbenefits and we need to show that without you know naming and shaming and making it public but I think that that's another important part of it and I think that's something which I think is a fairly recent development around the board table where you know the rubber is really hitting the road on that stuff.

And I think it's a, and we have really good examples of where we've done it, where we've removed local leadership, you know, after some difficult conversations, put somebody else in place and the thing has just gone boom and flourished. And again, we highlight those as examples of what happens when the right things are in place. So that's the joy of it. Shared learning. I would say one of our most successful programmes overseas is a mother and baby programme, which is now in six countries in Africa. We've just extended it to Ghana on the West Coast. The others are five countries in East Africa. It is an extraordinarily successful programme, reaching all over a million women, men and children in the last 10 years.

It provides pre and postnatal care. Make sure that women get into the system, get advice, go to clinics rather than trying to manage on their own, it improves the chances of having healthy babies and it improves the chances of the mothers not coming to harm during their pregnancies. It also provides contraceptive advice to women should they want it. So it involves the fathers in the process, which is a really, really important part of it for us. There is an extremely sophisticated monitoring and evaluation process that goes with it, so that we can see what works and what doesn't. And we are now using that model for a completely separate programme in the Caribbean, which is to do with training first-aiders, community first-aiders in communities in the Caribbean.

But the methodology is just being transferred because we've seen that it works. And that's a real example of that sort of shared learning and making sure that it is put to good use elsewhere in our family. And there are other instances, I think, where that would be possible, too. The North-South Money thing, our fundraising is not just for the Global South. I mean, there are programmes of every single one of our organisations as a charity. So, for example, there are programmes that my colleagues in Western Australia would like to carry out with the Indigenous communities there, which are remote and have serious health concerns and health challenges.

The money that they earn from their charitable work is not enough to fund some of these more ambitious programmes. So it is, you know, with the right focus, right at the heart and centre of our mission, it won't just go in that direction. So I hope that goes some way to undermining the idea that we're just we know we're sitting in London doling out monitor Africa and Caribbean associations and they're all involved in the process. I mean it's certainly not me or anybody on my team or the board deciding what is needed and some of them are very ambitious but need help to establish the basics first.

So I think that's the other thing that we're trying to do make them all self-sustaining in order to build up, you know, not overnight from where they are to being like St John Ambulance England. So I think that's important. And I told you about the relationship agreement at the beginning. So that's the government's piece.

turns.speaker: Kim Kucinskas

and some just won't and where I where I work we talk about each employee needs to get it want it and can do it and those are the three questions do you get it do you want it and maybe I as an employee got it five years ago but I just don't get the direction or maybe I'm saying that I want it but really in my heart of hearts the whole power shift thing isn't working for me so I feel like this is a tension or an elephant in the room, we don't talk about enough that we can't bring everyone along. turns.speaker: Susan le Jeune d'Allegeershecque
paras: Yeah, so I think, I don't think any of the progress and any of the transformation which has happened in St John in recent years would have happened without one person who is our most senior leader outside the Royal Family who is an Australian. He's worked in the private sector in health care for a long, long time. He came into this with a clear idea that things needed to change and he hasn't just made trends during this process, you know, but he recognises that everybody has a role as a part to play and he talks about, we've just had our AGM last week and he concluded by talking about a phenomenon which he'd seen in the past and I've seen this too, particularly in my old job, where people would come together for one of those big meetings and all nod the heads and say it was fantastic.

And on the plane, on the way home, and certainly when they got back to their home base, they'd start saying, oh, those people in London, oh, they just talk, I don't agree with any of it. But you know, I think we've, I think we've got beyond that. And I think that that is because he's such a brilliant leader. It's also because the leaders in our individual establishments have been have changed. He's had a personal role in making sure that the people who have been on the shortlist are the right sorts of people in an organisation like ours, there has been, there can be an element of you've been around for the right number of times and done the right number of right sorts of jobs so you automatically get the top job eventually.

That has meant that we have not been diverse in any way in our leadership in the past and that is also, I mean it's a slow process as you all know but that is changing too. We're also for the first time ever and I'm really pleased that this has happened because I mentioned it in my recruitment interview that it was something that was missing. We have a global leadership development programme so we bring together young middle career most of them people from across the St John family so you've got people from the Pacific, Papua New Guinea, the Caribbean, wherever, they come to London for a residential thing, then they have mentoring and they each bring a project that they want to work on.

Those people are much more diverse than our current leadership. They have been told that when they see things in their home establishments that are not right they are empowered to speak up and challenge them because that's part of the problem with an old relatively small c-conservative organisation like ours and I think the more that we can do that the better. So if you combine that with cracking down and dealing with poor leadership which doesn't abide by our values for whatever reason then I think you begin to send the message and the people who are attracted to those leadership positions also change because they see what they can get out of it.

And within my own small team, I've had significant turnover of staff. I mean, we haven't actually pushed anybody out of the door, but there are some people who probably didn't feel entirely comfortable with the direct, it's not really even the direction of travel, it's the way in which we are working and what we were being expected to deliver, you know, it's quite, it's quite the pressure is constant, and there's always something new. And we also need to show the trustees and the rest of the organisation in our value. So that means that there's always something that we need to do. And I think to go back to the point about, you know, sometimes you have to do things when not everybody agrees with you, absolutely right.

This resource hub that we set up, there was extreme scepticism when we floated the idea with the Board to start with. And now everybody thinks it's absolutely fantastic. So sometimes the executive, if the executive knows it's the right thing to do, probably just has to convince the chair or at least say just give us a go and then get on and do it. And what we now do at our AGM each year is we have a session where we report back on what we discussed last year and we show them and we done it. I think that creates that atmosphere of trust and confidence which I think is absolutely fundamental to all of this.

There is no way in which you are ever going to be be able to achieve change unless you have that trust, confidence and transparency. And not just to talk about the good stuff, we had a session, I'm not gonna go into the details, we had a session at the AGM where two of our establishments talked in great detail about some things that had gone wrong. And we all said five years ago that wouldn't have been possible. So I think that that's the other part of that picture, you know, that you leave your ego outside the door and you come in and you're honest and you're transparent about the challenges that you face so that we can all learn from each other.
